meters.label: Highest minus lowest kept count, out of 10,000 runs

frames.narration: A nightly export of 10,000 rows is already sorted, and the sort picks the first element as its pivot. Nothing is ever smaller than the pivot, so each split peels off a single row.
The cost is n(n-1)/2: 499,500 comparisons for 1,000 rows, 49,995,000 for 10,000. Sorted data is not an attack, just a common shape, and every cheap fixed pivot rule has some input like it.

Now the pivot comes from a seeded generator, chosen uniformly among the rows in the current part. The input order no longer matters: 154,586 comparisons for the same 10,000 sorted rows. On 1,000 rows, 20 different seeds cost between 10,113 and 11,960.

Expected, not guaranteed: the worst case is now a bad-luck event, not a bad input. And randomness has a price: on shuffled rows the first element took 146,101 comparisons, the random pivot 160,879. It is a Las Vegas algorithm: always correct, running time varies.

A second job needs 3 fair random lines from a log it can read only once. Keeping the first 3 is not random: over 10,000 runs on a stream of 10 items, the first 3 are kept 10,000 times each and the rest never.
"Replace a random slot half the time" looks fair and is not. A late item has to win one coin flip, an early one has to survive them all: counts from 1,679 to 4,928, where 3,000 is fair.

Reservoir sampling: item number i replaces a random cell with chance k/i. That chance falls as the stream grows, exactly offsetting the longer time early items have been exposed. Counts range from 2,915 to 3,071, around the fair 3,000.

It also scales: one pass over 1,000,000 items with k = 5 wrote to the reservoir only 64 times and held 5 cells instead of a million. Fix the seed in tests and log it; for anything an attacker gains by predicting, seed from the operating system's secure source, and use a cryptographically secure generator for secrets.
